and "his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the
city was full of idols" (v. 16).
What is the really superstitious element in this poly-
theistic worship? Might it for example be merely this,
namely, that heathen worship was based on false conceptions,
springing from a childish mode of thought, whereas
Christianity, with its teaching about the unity of God,
brought enlightenment and swept away all such false con-
ceptions by its essential truth and maturity of thought?
Certainly not. Paul could not have meant this, for the
simple reason that he knew that Greek culture had long ago
transcended the stage of polytheism, and that. Greek
philosophers taught, like Christianity, the unity of the God
who is immanent in the world, in whom "we live and move
and have our being"
', and to whom man is related in the
depths of his inner life. In fact he quotes a line from one of
the Greek philosophical poets, "For we are indeed His
offspring", which implies the offspring of the one God.
Those philosophers taught that the gods who are worshipped
in the various temples according to ancient custom are but
energies and emanations flowing from the primal Godhead
which is everywhere worshipped under a diversity of names.
Hence the struggle of Christianity against idolatry did not
consist in the fact that it had to remove, by its superior
enlightenment, false heathenish notions of God.
Hence what precisely is the superstitious element in
heathen religion? It consists in two factors.
1. Polytheism is an expression of man's fundamental
anxiety. The worship of gods arose of course from the fact
that the world is mysterious and uncanny for mankind.
Mysterious and uncanny are the forces of nature and the
caprices of fate, which sometimes lavish on man their
blessing, sometimes bring ruin and destruction; now pro-
moting his efforts, now frustrating them. Mysterious and
uncanny again are the forces which break out from the
depths of man's mind, his impulses and passions, leading him
